newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bundesbank's hands appear tied as mark falters.
newsitem.headline: Bundesbank's hands appear tied as mark falters.

text.p: Germany's Bundesbank has seemingly backed itself neatly into a corner.

The central bank has made abundantly clear that it is less than happy with the dollar's relentless surge against the mark and has signalled it will not hesitate to take action if it feels this trend is going too far too fast.

But financial markets, clearly bent on testing the central bank's resolve, have made equally clear that it will take more than a rise of a few basis points in German money market rates to change their bullish view on the dollar.

And although the central bank has hinted that it sees some bottlenecks building in the economy, it would be hard for it to justify a major interest rate rise on domestic grounds with unemployment running at 11.4 percent and inflation still low.

Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing on Tuesday became the latest central bank council member to spell out to markets that the bank is watching the mark's movements closely. The dollar has risen over 20 percent on the mark this year.

In an interview in the magazine Boerse Online -- published as the dollar jumped to an eight-year high over 1.88 marks -- Issing said: "The fact that the mark has weakened so fast and so significantly certainly gives us something to think about."

The central bank has stressed throughout that it is the speed of the mark's drop which concerns it rather than the actual lower value of the currency. The lower mark rate itself brings relief for the economy by boosting exports.
And while the Bonn government said on Wednesday it saw no need to dramatise the currency moves, the downtrend of recent days is probably steeper than the central bank would like.

The apparent dilemma for the Bundesbank is exacerbated by the fact that the bank itself kicked off an intense round of interest rate rise speculation almost two weeks ago, as its central bank council deliberately left its policy course open for the second half of a four-week summer break.

The council followed a now-established pattern of announcing that its next two securities repurchase tenders -- the regular flow of central bank funds to the banking system -- would be set at an unchanged interest rate of three percent.

But it made no comment on its plans for policy from next week, leading markets to speculate the bank could be preparing to nudge rates higher by setting a variable rate repurchase tender or simply offering a repo at a higher fixed rate.
In a variable rate repo banks bid for funds at the interest rates of their choice rather than accepting a pre-set rate.
Although the Bundesbank studiously avoided any promise of a rate rise, financial markets believed the message was clear.
Yet this week's money market operations signalled a neutral policy stance. The Bundesbank added 2.6 billion marks to the market in this week's repo, more than dealers had expected.
The market concluded no early rate rise was on the cards.
This, analysts say, is not surprising under the current circumstances, where dollar bulls are clearly indulging in a spot of Bundesbank-baiting -- daring the bank to take action.
With the market in this sort of mood, any cosmetic upward move on interest rates could simply be shrugged off, maybe even causing a loss of credibility for the central bank, they said.
"The Bundesbank would have to do more than the domestic economy can withstand to engineer a downward dollar correction," said Ulrich Beckmann, an economist at Deutsche Bank Research in Frankfurt.

"I think that they will stick with a further repo at three percent next week. If the dollar climbs much further they could add a variable repo alongside. But that would only be a means to signal their concern, not to turn the dollar round."

Some analysts argue the Bundesbank's decision to keep the option of a rate rise in the middle of the summer had in itself proved a miscalculation, worsening the mark's problems by fuelling traders' zeal to force the Bundesbank's hand.
The July 24 decisions came at a dollar rate of about 1.8350 marks, five pfennigs below the current rate of around 1.8850.

"The Bundesbank opened the floodgates to this situation," said Sally Wilkinson, senior international economist at Daiwa Europe. "Without this decision we would not have seen such a big weakening as the market would not have pushed so hard."

With a small interest rate rise judged potentially ineffective, and no domestic justification for a large one, the Bundesbank looks powerless to use monetary policy if it is indeed sufficiently concerned to take action to shore up the mark.
But its options to protest look even more limited.

Intervention to buy marks in the market would only stand any chance of working if other major world players -- at the very least the United States Federal Reserve and probably the Bank of Japan -- joined forces to push the dollar lower.
But even verbal intervention by these countries to suppport the mark has so far been conspicuous only by its absence.
